slides.title: Tokenisation
slides.text: Session 1 Tokenisation Explain how a subword tokeniser splits Arabic, Arabizi and English text Measure tokens per message and price the difference by variety Normalise alef, hamza, ta marbuta, diacritics and digits, and trace a failure to its cause 01

slides.title: A model never sees text: it sees a list of integers
slides.text: Tokenisation A model never sees text: it sees a list of integers Text The meter is broken → Pieces The · meter · is · broken → Ids 785 · 16430 · 318 · 5445 → Vectors one row of a table per id The tokeniser is fixed before training and shipped with the model: change it and the model reads noise. Everything a provider counts and charges is tokens, not words or characters.

slides.title: Subwords sit between characters and words
slides.text: The unit Subwords sit between characters and words Unit Vocabulary A new word Length of a message Characters or bytes tiny always representable very long Whole words millions, never complete unknown short Subwords 30,000 to 250,000 built from pieces in between tokenisationالفاتورة A frequent word is one piece. A rare word is several. A word from a language the tokeniser rarely saw is many.

slides.title: Byte-pair encoding merges the most frequent pair, again and again
slides.text: How a vocabulary is learnt Byte-pair encoding merges the most frequent pair, again and again Start from single characters or bytes. Count every adjacent pair in the training text. Merge the most frequent pair into one new piece. Repeat until the vocabulary has the size you asked for. What the merges remember The training text. English web text gives English pieces; Arabic text gives Arabic pieces. WordPiece The same idea with another score; it marks a continuing piece with ## and has an [UNK] piece.

slides.title: The same complaint costs a different number of tokens in each variety
slides.text: Measured in Lab 1.1 · 50 parallel messages The same complaint costs a different number of tokens in each variety Tokeniser MSA Gulf Arabizi English GPT-2 (English web text) 40.1 32.7 18.8 11.8 Qwen3 (multilingual) 15.0 14.6 19.4 11.9 CAMeLBERT-mix (Arabic) 9.7 8.7 25.5 23.6 Mean tokens per message. Same facts in every column. No row is good at Arabizi. Nobody trained a tokeniser on it, so every tokeniser spells it out.

slides.title: A tokeniser that never saw Arabic falls back to bytes
slides.text: Why 40 tokens A tokeniser that never saw Arabic falls back to bytes 5.3 GPT-2 tokens per MSA word 2.0 Qwen3 tokens per MSA word 1.3 CAMeLBERT tokens per MSA word An Arabic letter is two bytes in UTF-8. With no merged pieces, a five-letter word is up to ten tokens. Nothing breaks and nothing is unknown: the message is only three times longer, slower and more expensive.

slides.title: Price the difference, then look at what you are paying for
slides.text: Tokens are money Price the difference, then look at what you are paying for Variety Message only With a 180-token prompt MSA 0.0030 0.0390 Gulf 0.0029 0.0389 Arabizi 0.0039 0.0399 English 0.0024 0.0384 Message only Arabizi costs 1.62 times English. With the instructions The prompt is over 90% of the bill in every variety. USD per 1,000 messages at 0.20 USD per million input tokens, Qwen3 token counts.

slides.title: One word, many spellings: normalise before you match or count
slides.text: Arabic orthography One word, many spellings: normalise before you match or count What varies As written Normalised to Diacritics and shadda العَدّاد العداد Tatweel, the stretching mark العـداد العداد Alef with hamza أرجو · إغلاق ارجو · اغلاق Ta marbuta written as ha الفاتورة · الفاتوره الفاتوره Alef maqsura for ya فى في Arabic-Indic digits ٣٠٦١٠٧٤٦١٠ 3061074610 Normalise for matching, keep the original for display. The customer wrote it their way.

slides.title: Two failures, each traced to its cause
slides.text: Measured in Lab 1.1 Two failures, each traced to its cause One diacritic, one unknown word العَدّاد becomes [UNK] for the Arabic tokeniser and 9 pieces instead of 5 for the multilingual one. Cause. The training text had no diacritics, so no piece contains one. An account number at twice the price A sentence with ٣٠٦١٠٧٤٦١٠ costs 25 tokens; with Western digits, 15. Cause. Each Arabic-Indic digit is two bytes with no merged piece. 1,052 → 0 unknown pieces in 1,340 Arabic-script messages, before and after normalising 2,968 → 1,760 distinct word forms, before and after

slides.title: Arabizi has no spelling, so every writer invents one
slides.text: Dialect and Latin script Arabizi has no spelling, so every writer invents one Digit Letter Example 3 ع 3adad (meter) 7 ح 7sab (account) 5 خ 5azan (tank) 6 · 9 ط · ص 6ag6 (pressure) · 9a3eef (weak) The same word arrives as 3adad, aadad, adad: the archive has all three. Dialect changes the words too: الماء is الماي or المويه in Gulf messages. No tokeniser, and few models, were trained on it. Expect it to be the worst column of every table this week.

slides.title: Which change cuts the token bill most?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which change cuts the token bill most? Sawaqi routes 60,000 messages a month with a hosted model. Each call sends 180 tokens of instructions and a message of about 15 tokens. Which single change cuts the bill most? Translating Arabizi messages to English first Removing diacritics and tatweel from every message Shortening the instructions from 180 to 90 tokens Switching the hosted model to an Arabic tokeniser

slides.title: Embeddings and semantic search
slides.text: Session 2 Embeddings and semantic search Explain what an embedding and cosine similarity capture Index a message archive and answer queries with a vector index Score recall at 10 for each language variety and read where it fails 02

slides.title: An embedding puts a text at a point; close points mean close meanings
slides.text: Embeddings An embedding puts a text at a point; close points mean close meanings A token id selects a row of a table: its embedding. A model mixes the rows of a message into one vector for the whole message. Trained so that texts used alike land close together. A multilingual model lands a message and its translation close together. Close الماي مقطوع · no water at home · el mai maqtoo3 Far no water at home · I was charged twice

slides.title: With unit vectors, similarity is one dot product
slides.text: Similarity With unit vectors, similarity is one dot product # E: (2000, d), each row of length 1 E = G.embed(messages) q = G.embed([query])[0] # (d,) # cosine similarity, 2000 at once scores = E @ q top = np.argsort(-scores)[:10] Cosine similarity compares directions and ignores length: 1 the same, 0 unrelated. Normalise every vector to length 1 once; then cosine is the dot product. One matrix multiplication scores a query against the whole archive.

slides.title: Choose an embedding model on your own queries, in your own varieties
slides.text: Which model Choose an embedding model on your own queries, in your own varieties Question Why it matters at Sawaqi Which languages was it trained on? An English-only model sees Arabic as noise Are the weights open, and under which licence? You may need to run it yourself later How long a text does it take, how many dimensions? Messages are short; memory is rows × dimensions Where does it run, and what leaves the building? Message text carries personal data What does it score on your 40 queries? A public leaderboard has no Gulf Arabizi

slides.title: Index once, offline; answer every query online
slides.text: The shape of every search system Index once, offline; answer every query online Offline normalise and embed 2,000 messages → Index store the vectors with their message ids → Online embed the query with the same model → Search top 10 by similarity Flat index Compare with every row. Exact. Fine to about a million rows. Approximate index Visit a fraction of the rows (FAISS, LanceDB). Faster, and it can miss: measure its recall too.

slides.title: Recall at 10: of the relevant messages a top-10 list could hold, how many it holds
slides.text: The metric Recall at 10: of the relevant messages a top-10 list could hold, how many it holds query el majari 6af7a fi el rabwa relevant 8 messages: sewage overflow in Al-Rabwa, in any variety top 10 holds 2 of them recall at 10 2 / min(10, 8) = 0.25 Divide by min(10, relevant): a list of ten cannot hold fifteen. Average over the queries of one variety, then report the four numbers side by side. Relevance here is a rule (same complaint type, same district). In production it is a person's judgement, and it costs time.

slides.title: A character n-gram baseline finds its own script and little else
slides.text: Measured in Lab 1.2 · 20 queries A character n-gram baseline finds its own script and little else English 0.40 MSA 0.33 Gulf 0.29 Arabizi 0.02 Recall at 10 of TF-IDF over character 2- to 4-grams, no model. The relevant messages are in all four varieties; shared letters find only the query's own. Arabizi: every writer spells differently, so even its own script fails. Your embedding model's row goes next to this one. That table is the evidence.

slides.title: Semantic search fails where there is no meaning to embed
slides.text: Know the tool's edge Semantic search fails where there is no meaning to embed Identifiers An account number, a ticket, a meter serial. Use an exact lookup. Negation and numbers "No leak" and "a leak" are close. So are 14 days and 41 days. Rare varieties What the model rarely saw lands in the wrong place. Measure it per variety. Hybrid. Run an exact or keyword search beside the vector search and merge the two rankings. The lab's stretch does it in eight lines.

slides.title: An agent searches for an account number and gets nonsense
slides.text: Checkpoint An agent searches for an account number and gets nonsense Hessa's agents type an account number into Ghayth's semantic search and get ten unrelated messages. The same search works well for "brown water in Al-Qalaa". What do you change? Add an exact lookup on the account number beside the vector search Move to a larger embedding model Replace the approximate index by a flat one Embed each message together with its customer's name

slides.title: Semantic search over 2,000 messages
slides.text: Lab 1.2 · 25 min Semantic search over 2,000 messages Index 2,000 messages with an open multilingual embedding model and score 20 queries by variety, against a character n-gram baseline. D1_2_semantic_search.ipynb Normalise and build a character n-gram baseline 6 min Embed 2,000 messages with a hosted open model 6 min A flat inner-product index and one query 5 min Recall at 10 for 20 queries, by variety 8 min ✱ Stretch: Score all 40 queries and add a hybrid of both rankings

slides.title: Inside the transformer
slides.text: Session 3 Inside the transformer Describe attention as queries, keys and values Read an attention map for one Arabic sentence Explain when an encoder and when a decoder fits the task 03

slides.title: Every token asks, every token offers, and each takes a weighted mix
slides.text: Attention Every token asks, every token offers, and each takes a weighted mix Query What this token is looking for. Key What each token offers to be found by. Value What a token hands over when it is chosen. weights = softmax(Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k)) # (tokens, tokens): each row sums to 1 output = weights @ V # each token: a weighted average of the values

slides.title: Attention is eight lines, and the lab checks yours against the model's
slides.text: Lab 1.3, step 2 Attention is eight lines, and the lab checks yours against the model's def attention_weights(q, k, causal=False): scores = q @ k.T / math.sqrt(q.shape[-1]) if causal: # a decoder may not look ahead seen = torch.ones_like(scores).tril().bool() scores = scores.masked_fill(~seen, -math.inf) return scores.softmax(-1) Dividing by the square root of the head's width keeps the softmax from saturating. The causal mask is the only difference between an encoder's attention and a decoder's. The check: your weights equal the model's own for layer 0, head 0, to five decimals.

slides.title: A transformer is that operation, several heads wide and several layers deep
slides.text: The whole model A transformer is that operation, several heads wide and several layers deep Token and position embeddings one vector per token ↓ Attention, several heads each head looks for something else ↓ Feed-forward layer each token on its own ↓ Repeat for every layer then a head for the task The course encoder Value Layers × heads 2 × 4 Width 128 Vocabulary 2,000 Parameters 529,408 Of which token embeddings 256,000

slides.title: An encoder reads both ways; a decoder only looks back
slides.text: One mask apart An encoder reads both ways; a decoder only looks back Encoder Every token attends to every token. In the lab's sentence, 36% of the first layer's attention goes to later tokens. Trained to fill in a hidden token from both sides. Decoder A token attends to itself and earlier tokens. Attention to later tokens: exactly 0. Trained to predict the next token from the left side. An attention map shows where a head looked. It is not an explanation of the model's decision.

slides.title: Fill the gap, or predict what comes next
slides.text: Measured in Lab 1.3 Fill the gap, or predict what comes next encoder the water [MASK] is very weak on the second floor fills "pressure" first: it has read the rest of the sentence decoder the water continues several openings stay likely: smells, coming, pressure, was A decision about a whole message wants the whole message in view: an encoder with a small head. Writing text token by token is what a decoder is for; it can also be asked to decide, at a price.

slides.title: Match the family to the job before you match the model
slides.text: Choosing a family Match the family to the job before you match the model Job at Sawaqi Family Why Route a message to one of eight departments Encoder + classification head One pass, eight scores, milliseconds on a processor Tag each word (a district, an account number) Encoder + token-classification head One score per token Find similar messages Encoder trained for embeddings One vector per message Draft a reply, extract into JSON without training data Decoder, prompted Writes text; needs no labels; costs per token

slides.title: Two million messages a day, eight departments
slides.text: Checkpoint Two million messages a day, eight departments A national utility must label 2 million messages a day with one of eight departments, on its own servers without graphics processors, and has 50,000 labelled messages. Which design fits? A large prompted decoder that writes the department name An encoder-decoder that translates the message into a label An embedding model and a search over all labelled messages A small encoder with a classification head, fine-tuned on the labels

slides.title: Attention in an encoder and a decoder
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · 25 min Attention in an encoder and a decoder Inspect attention for one Arabic sentence in the course encoder and decoder, compare what each token can see, and compare filling a gap with predicting the next token. D1_3_attention.ipynb Load the course encoder and decoder 4 min Attention by hand for one head 7 min Read the maps: who attends to whom 7 min Fill the gap, or predict the next token 7 min ✱ Stretch: Change one letter of the sentence and compare the maps

slides.title: Decision models
slides.text: Session 4 Decision models Build a bag-of-words linear classifier without AI assistance Report macro F1 and F1 by language variety Decide when a classifier should abstain 04

slides.title: Most language work in production is a decision, not a paragraph
slides.text: Decision models Most language work in production is a decision, not a paragraph Classification One label for a message: a department, urgent or not, a language variety. Token classification One label per word: this is a district, this is an account number. Ranking An order over candidates: which earlier messages are most alike. A decision has a right answer, so it can be scored on thousands of examples. It runs on every message, so its latency and cost are multiplied by the volume.

slides.title: Build the cheapest thing that could work, and make everything else beat it
slides.text: Baselines first Build the cheapest thing that could work, and make everything else beat it It takes an hour and sets the floor. It shows whether the labels and the split are sound before a larger model hides the problem. It is the fallback when the larger model is down, slow or withdrawn. Sometimes it wins. Then you are done. Without a baseline "The model scores 0.84" means nothing. Is that 20 points above word counts, or 1 point below?

slides.title: Count words and character n-grams; weigh the rare ones up
slides.text: The baseline's eyes Count words and character n-grams; weigh the rare ones up make_union( # words and pairs of words TfidfVectorizer(preprocessor=G.normalise, ngram_range=(1, 2)), # pieces of words, 2 to 4 characters TfidfVectorizer(preprocessor=G.normalise, analyzer="char_wb", ngram_range=(2, 4))) # then LogisticRegression(C=10, max_iter=1000) TF-IDF : a word counts more when few messages contain it. Character n-grams survive a typo, a glued prefix (بالفاتوره) and an Arabizi spelling that varies. A linear model gives each feature one weight per department: you can read why it decided. 400 messages give 13,005 features.

slides.title: Macro F1 gives every department one vote, however small
slides.text: The metric, by hand Macro F1 gives every department one vote, however small Department Precision Recall F1 billing (large) 0.90 0.90 0.90 supply (large) 0.80 1.00 0.89 connections (small) 1.00 0.20 0.33 Macro F1 0.71 Precision : of the messages sent to a department, how many belonged there. Recall : of the messages that belonged there, how many arrived. F1 = 2PR / (P + R). Macro: the plain mean over departments. Accuracy would hide the small department; macro F1 puts it on the slide.

slides.title: The baseline scores 0.85, and half of that for Arabizi
slides.text: Measured in Lab 1.4 · 403 test messages The baseline scores 0.85, and half of that for Arabizi All 0.85 MSA 0.94 Gulf 0.86 English 0.81 Arabizi 0.42 4 ms median per message on one laptop processor; 5 ms at the 95th percentile Report every row "0.85" is true and hides one customer in eight.

slides.title: A model cannot learn a pair it has no examples of
slides.text: Why Arabizi fails A model cannot learn a pair it has no examples of Department Arabizi messages in training Arabizi test messages right supply 11 8 of 16 billing 7 9 of 10 meters 4 4 of 7 quality 2 0 of 3 wastewater 0 0 of 2 Accuracy on Arabizi is 0.57; macro F1 is 0.42, because the empty departments count in full. The fix is not a cleverer model first. It is labels where there are none, or a person for those messages.

slides.title: Below a confidence threshold, hand the message to a person
slides.text: A router may say "I do not know" Below a confidence threshold, hand the message to a person Threshold Handed off Accuracy on the rest 0.3 40 of 403 0.94 0.4 79 0.97 0.5 128 0.98 0.6 168 1.00 Every point on this table is a staffing decision: people cost more than mistakes, or the reverse. At 0.5, 31 of the 51 Arabizi messages go to a person. The threshold belongs in the model card, with its hand-off rate. Day 3 writes it there.

slides.title: One number went up. Did the router get better?
slides.text: Checkpoint One number went up. Did the router get better? A new version raises test macro F1 from 0.85 to 0.87: MSA 0.94 to 0.97, Gulf 0.86 to 0.90, English 0.81 to 0.84, Arabizi 0.42 to 0.31. What do you report? An improvement of two points, ready to ship A gain for three varieties, a loss for Arabizi, and a hand-off rule for Arabizi No real change, since the Arabizi test set is too small to matter A regression that must be rolled back in full

slides.title: Text became numbers, and you have a number to beat
slides.text: Day 1 recap Text became numbers, and you have a number to beat Tokens are the unit of cost; the same message costs up to three times more in a variety the tokeniser never saw. Normalise before matching: 1,052 unknown pieces became 0. Embeddings search by meaning; identifiers need an exact lookup. Attention : an encoder reads both ways, a decoder looks back. Baseline : macro F1 0.85, Arabizi 0.42, 4 ms a message. Report by variety , always.

slides.title: Before we generate anything
slides.text: Review · Day 1 Before we generate anything A message contains العَدّاد with diacritics. The Arabic tokeniser returns [UNK] and the router sends the message to the wrong department. Where is the fix? Retrain the router with more epochs Ask for a tokeniser with a larger vocabulary Leave it, since diacritics are rare in customer messages Normalise the text before the tokeniser sees it

slides.title: Generative language models
slides.text: Session 1 Generative language models Explain how temperature and top-p change the next-token choice Measure the consistency of replies across repeated samples Detect details a reply invented 01

slides.title: A generative model is yesterday's decoder in a loop
slides.text: Generative language models A generative model is yesterday's decoder in a loop Context the tokens so far → Decoder one score per vocabulary entry → Sampling scores become one chosen token → Append and go round again The model never writes a sentence. It scores the next token, thousands of times. Everything it "knows" at a step is in the context: your instructions, the message, and what it has written so far. It stops at an end token or at your max_tokens.

slides.title: A chat is one long text with markers the model was trained to follow
slides.text: Base and instruction-tuned A chat is one long text with markers the model was trained to follow system You write short replies for the contact centre of Sawaqi. Use only the facts given. user Customer message: … FACTS: {"ticket": "SW-48211", "crew_eta_hours": 4} assistant the model continues from here A base model continues any text. An instruction-tuned model was trained further on conversations in one fixed format. The provider's chat template turns your list of messages into that format. Use the API's roles; do not write the markers yourself. The system message is not a law. It is text the model was trained to weigh heavily.

slides.title: Temperature sharpens or flattens the same scores
slides.text: Measured in Lab 2.1 on the course decoder Temperature sharpens or flattens the same scores Temperature Probability of the top token Entropy (bits) Reads as 0.2 0.996 0.04 almost always the same token 0.7 0.631 2.42 the favourite, with variety 1.0 0.335 4.97 the model's own distribution 1.5 0.108 7.63 unlikely tokens get drawn Next token after الماي ("the water"). The scores are divided by the temperature before the softmax. At 0, providers take the top token.

slides.title: Top-p removes the long tail before the draw
slides.text: Nucleus sampling Top-p removes the long tail before the draw probs = (logits / temperature).softmax(-1) order = probs.argsort(descending=True) before = probs[order].cumsum(0) - probs[order] # the smallest set that reaches top_p keep = order[before < top_p] out = torch.zeros_like(probs) out[keep] = probs[keep] out = out / out.sum() Thousands of unlikely tokens together hold real probability. One of them, drawn, is the odd word in a reply. At temperature 1.0, top_p=0.9 leaves 73 tokens of 2,000; top_p=0.5 leaves 3. Use one knob at a time, and write down both.

slides.title: Consistency is a number: generate twice, compare
slides.text: Lab 2.1, steps 2 and 3 Consistency is a number: generate twice, compare Setting Temperature Top-p Exact agreement · word overlap focused 0.0 1.0 measured by your run: ten tasks, two samples each balanced 0.7 0.9 loose 1.3 1.0 Exact agreement : the share of sample pairs with identical text. Word overlap : shared words over all words of the pair. A reply a customer could receive in two versions is a complaint waiting to happen. Decide how much variation the task tolerates, then set the knobs.

slides.title: An invented detail is anything stated that the inputs do not hold
slides.text: Lab 2.1, step 4 An invented detail is anything stated that the inputs do not hold Factsticket SW-48211, crew within 4 hours ReplyYour request is logged as SW-48211. A crew will reach you within 4 hours. ReplyYour request is logged as SW-48211. You will receive a credit of 50 SAR under rule R-11. The model is completing a plausible reply. A credit is plausible. A regular expression catches the costly kind: numbers and identifiers that are in neither the message nor the facts. It does not catch an invented promise in words. That needs a person or a second model, and a sample to read.

slides.title: Set the knobs by what a wrong output costs
slides.text: Choosing settings Set the knobs by what a wrong output costs Task Setting Then check with code Route to a department temperature 0, a dozen output tokens the label is one of eight Extract fields temperature 0, JSON mode schema and validators Answer from the rule book temperature 0 citation present, refusal exact Draft a reply for an agent to send moderate temperature, top-p below 1 no number or identifier outside the facts Temperature 0 makes a model repeat itself, not tell the truth. A repeated invented detail is still invented.

slides.text: Checkpoint The same message, a different department each run Ghayth routes with a prompted model. The same message is sent to billing on one run and to meters on the next. slides.title: A prompt is a specification: say what, from what, and in which shape
slides.text: Prompting A prompt is a specification: say what, from what, and in which shape You extract fields from one customer message of a water utility. The message may be in Modern Standard Arabic, Gulf dialect, Arabic in Latin script or English. Personal values are masked as [ACCOUNT_n], [PHONE_n], [NAME_n]. Return JSON only, with exactly these keys: account_number, district (one of eight, or null), complaint_type (one of sixteen). Never invent a value. TaskInput, and what is unusual about itOutput contractThe rule that code will check

slides.title: Mask personal fields before the text leaves, and put them back after
slides.text: Personal data Mask personal fields before the text leaves, and put them back after message انا عبدالله الشمري، ارغب في تقسيط مبلغ 425 ريال، حسابي رقم ٣٠٨٢٨٢٨٥١٣ masked انا [NAME_1] [NAME_2]، ارغب في تقسيط مبلغ 425 ريال، حسابي رقم [ACCOUNT_1] model {"account_number": "[ACCOUNT_1]", "district": null, "complaint_type": "installment_request"} unmasked account_number = "3082828513", inside Sawaqi The model needs to know where the account number is, not what it is. Sawaqi's rule R-10 classifies customer records as Restricted and requires this step.

slides.title: A masking step without a test is a hope
slides.text: Measured in Lab 2.2 A masking step without a test is a hope 200 messages masked 0 with a 10-digit run or a known name left 200 restored exactly by unmasking Arabic-Indic digits are turned into Western digits first: a pattern for 30 and eight digits must find ٣٠ too. The test proves the patterns on these messages. It cannot see a name outside the list or a phone number written with spaces: say so in the card.

slides.title: The schema is the contract; validators check values, not only shapes
slides.text: Structured outputs The schema is the contract; validators check values, not only shapes class Extraction(BaseModel, extra="forbid"): account_number: Optional[str] district: Optional[District] # one of eight complaint_type: ComplaintType # one of sixteen @field_validator("account_number") @classmethod def known_account(cls, value, info): mapping = info.context["mapping"] if value is not None and value not in mapping: raise ValueError("must be an [ACCOUNT_n] " "placeholder from the message") return value Types reject a wrong shape: a missing key, a district outside the list. The validator rejects a wrong value: an account number the model never saw, a phone placeholder in the account field. The error message is written for the model: it is sent back in the repair call.

slides.title: Validate, repair once, then log and hand off
slides.text: The loop around the model Validate, repair once, then log and hand off Mask placeholders in → Ask temperature 0, JSON mode → Validate schema and validators → Repair once send the error back → Log still failing: to a person The log is evidence Message id, attempt, error. It shows what the validators stopped, and which errors repair does not fix. Never guess A message that fails twice gets no fields. A wrong account number is worse than none.

slides.title: Valid JSON every time is a format guarantee, not a correctness guarantee
slides.text: Constrained output Valid JSON every time is a format guarantee, not a correctness guarantee JSON mode asks the model for JSON; constrained decoding removes every token that would break your schema. Both end parse errors. Neither knows which district the customer lives in. So measure values against gold fields: precision and recall for each field. For one field Counts as Right value returned correct Value returned, gold has none costs precision Null returned, gold has a value costs recall Wrong value returned costs both

slides.title: The baseline for extraction is three regular expressions, and it has two bugs
slides.text: Measured in Lab 2.2 · 200 messages with gold fields The baseline for extraction is three regular expressions, and it has two bugs Field Precision Recall Account number 0.69 0.76 District 0.97 0.97 Complaint type (keywords) 0.58 0.58 A number in Arabic-Indic digits is returned as written and does not equal the gold value. A message with a phone number and no account number returns the phone number. The district is easy; the complaint type is where a model can earn its cost. Your model's rows go beside these.

slides.title: The provider now guarantees schema-valid JSON
slides.text: Checkpoint The provider now guarantees schema-valid JSON You switch on constrained decoding. Every reply now parses and matches the schema. Which check can you still not drop? That every reply has the three keys That the district is one of the eight in the list That the account placeholder is one that occurs in this message That the reply is JSON and nothing else

slides.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
slides.text: Session 3 Retrieval-augmented generation Chunk and index a bilingual rule book Write a prompt that cites its sources and refuses when they are silent Evaluate retrieval and generation separately 03

slides.title: Facts that change live in documents, not in weights
slides.text: Retrieval-augmented generation Facts that change live in documents, not in weights CustomerHow much does a meter test cost and when is it refunded? Model aloneA plausible price, from nowhere. Model with rule R-07The answer the rule gives, with [R-07] after it. The tariff rule book is Latifa's: ten rules, each in English and Arabic. No model was trained on it, and it changes every quarter. Retrieve the rule, put it in the context, ask for an answer from it, with a citation.

slides.title: Two pipelines: one when the rules change, one for every question
slides.text: The shape Two pipelines: one when the rules change, one for every question Ingest · when the rule book changes split each rule into chunks, keep the rule id ↓ Index normalised words, or embeddings Answer · for every question retrieve the top 3 chunks ↓ Generate answer from them, cite, or refuse ↓ Check citation present, refusal exact

slides.title: For ten rules, a keyword search with Arabic normalisation finds every answer
slides.text: Measured in Lab 2.3 For ten rules, a keyword search with Arabic normalisation finds every answer 12 of 12 answerable questions with the right rule in the top 3 (English, MSA and Gulf) And nothing for Arabizi bkam tif7soon el 3adad? shares no word with a rule book in Arabic script and English. BM25 : a rare word counts more, a repeated word counts less each time, a long chunk gets no bonus. Normalise first, and cut words to six letters so that a word meets its suffixed forms. Start with the simplest retriever and an evaluation set. Add embeddings where the set shows a gap.

slides.title: Answer from the rules, cite the rule, or say the rules are silent
slides.text: The generator's contract Answer from the rules, cite the rule, or say the rules are silent You answer customers of Sawaqi Water Company from the RULES given in the message and from nothing else. Answer in the language of the question, in one or two sentences, and cite the rule you used in square brackets, like [R-02]. If the RULES do not answer the question, reply exactly: NOT_IN_RULES SourceFormCitationRefusal The user message holds the three retrieved chunks, each starting with its rule id, then the question.

slides.title: Score the retriever and the generator apart
slides.text: Lab 2.3, step 4 Score the retriever and the generator apart Number Over The part it measures Hit at 3 12 answerable questions the retriever: is the right rule in the context? Cited the right rule 12 answerable the generator: did it use that rule? Contains the key fact 12 answerable the generator: did it copy the figure correctly? False refusals 12 answerable the generator: too cautious Refused 4 questions the rules do not answer the generator: not cautious enough when below 4 One score for the whole pipeline cannot tell you which part to fix.

slides.title: Locate the error before you change anything
slides.text: Reading a wrong answer Locate the error before you change anything The rule was not retrieved Fix the retriever: wording, normalisation, a second search. The generator never had a chance. Retrieved, answer wrong Fix the prompt or the chunk: two tiers in one sentence, a figure copied from the wrong tier. Silent question, answered Read which retrieved rule it leaned on. Tighten the refusal clause; test it on more silent questions.

slides.title: The right rule, the wrong price
slides.text: Checkpoint The right rule, the wrong price A customer asks what the second residential tier costs. The top chunk is R-02, which lists all four tiers. The reply says "SAR 1.20 [R-02]"; the rule says SAR 2.50. Where do you look first? At the generator: the prompt and how the four tiers read in one sentence At the retriever: return ten chunks instead of three At the index: replace keywords by embeddings At the model: fine-tune it on the rule book

slides.title: Model selection and evaluation
slides.text: Session 4 Model selection and evaluation Compare models on one labelled set by macro F1 and F1 by variety Measure latency percentiles and cost per thousand messages Defend a choice against a latency budget 04

slides.title: A model is chosen on four columns, and a leaderboard has one
slides.text: Model selection A model is chosen on four columns, and a leaderboard has one Quality Macro F1 on your test set, and by variety. Latency Median and 95th percentile, against a budget. Cost Per 1,000 messages at your volume. Licence and place May you run the weights yourself? Where is the text processed? A public leaderboard ranks models on someone else's task, in someone else's language, with no price. Use it to choose candidates, never to choose.

slides.title: Cost = messages × tokens per call × the published price
slides.text: Cost Cost = messages × tokens per call × the published price Model (paid endpoint) Input, USD per million tokens Output The larger model of the lab 0.20 0.40 The smaller model of the lab 0.08 0.20 The baseline your own processor A routing call is about 200 input tokens and a few output tokens. At 0.20 per million: about 0.04 USD per 1,000 messages, 2.40 USD a month at 60,000 messages. A free endpoint costs nothing and has a daily request limit: price the paid endpoint of the same model.

slides.title: Latency is a distribution: report the median and the 95th percentile
slides.text: Latency Latency is a distribution: report the median and the 95th percentile The median (p50) is what a typical message waits. The 95th percentile (p95) is what one message in twenty waits. Budgets are written on it. A hosted model's latency includes the network and a queue you do not control. Sawaqi's budget: 300 ms at p95 per message. 4 · 5 ms the baseline's p50 and p95 on a laptop processor (Lab 1.4) A mean hides the queue Nineteen fast calls and one of five seconds average to "fine".

slides.title: Describe the eight departments, ask for one name, parse what comes back
slides.text: The prompted model as a classifier Describe the eight departments, ask for one name, parse what comes back SYSTEM = """You route one customer message of a water utility to one department. ... Departments: - billing: a bill that is too high, a charge twice - meters: a meter that is broken or reads wrong ... Reply with the department name only.""" def parse_label(reply): low = reply.lower() found = [(low.index(d), d) for d in DEPARTMENTS if d in low] return min(found)[1] if found else None No training data : the descriptions are the whole "training". Parse leniently ("Department: leaks"), and count a reply with no department as wrong. Temperature 0, a dozen output tokens.

slides.title: Forty messages, ten per variety: enough to find failures, not to rank close models
slides.text: Measured in Lab 2.4 · the baseline's row Forty messages, ten per variety: enough to find failures, not to rank close models Approach Macro F1 MSA Gulf Arabizi English Baseline, on these 40 0.81 1.00 0.60 0.51 0.71 Baseline, on all 403 0.85 0.94 0.86 0.42 0.81 Larger model measured by your run Smaller model The same baseline scores 0.60 for Gulf on ten messages and 0.86 on 157. With ten messages, one error moves a variety by several points. Read the errors, then widen the sample before you sign a decision.

slides.title: A cascade sends only the unsure messages to the expensive model
slides.text: You do not have to choose one A cascade sends only the unsure messages to the expensive model Baseline 4 ms, free → Confident? above a threshold: done → Prompted model the rest of the messages → Still unsure? to a person Cost and latency are paid only for the share of messages that reach the second step. The threshold is chosen on validation data, and its hand-off rate is reported. It is a new system: evaluate it as a whole, by variety, like any other row.

slides.title: A decision is three sentences someone can disagree with
slides.text: The output of model selection A decision is three sentences someone can disagree with Which approach routes today, and on which numbers. What it costs a month at Sawaqi's volume, and its p95 against the budget. Which messages go to a person until a better model exists. Say what would change it "If Arabizi F1 of the prompted model stays above the baseline's on 400 messages, we switch that variety." And what is not in the table Licence, where the text is processed, what happens when the model is withdrawn.

slides.title: The cheaper model ties on English
slides.text: Checkpoint The cheaper model ties on English The smaller model matches the larger one on English and MSA, loses 20 points on Arabizi, and costs less than half. 15% of messages are Arabizi. What do you recommend? The smaller model for everything, since it costs less than half The larger model for everything, since it is better somewhere Either one, since the two models are equivalent Route by variety: the larger model or a person for Arabizi; confirm on more messages

Thanks. 274 near-duplicate pairs within customers 29% of labelled messages have at least one near-duplicate

slides.title: A random split tests the model on messages it has nearly seen
slides.text: Measured in Lab 3.1 · five seeds each A random split tests the model on messages it has nearly seen Split Test messages with a near-copy in training Macro F1 Random 16% 0.892 By customer 0% 0.859 Same data, same baseline, same sizes: 400 to train, 400 to test. The model did not get better. The test got easier. The 0.033 of difference is a score no new customer will ever see. A larger model memorises better, so it profits more from the leak.

slides.title: Split by the unit that repeats, and give each part one job
slides.text: The rule Split by the unit that repeats, and give each part one job ids = df["customer_id"].drop_duplicates() \ .sample(frac=1, random_state=seed) sizes = df["customer_id"].value_counts() side, n_test, n_train = {}, 0, 0 for cid in ids: # a customer goes whole if n_test < 400: side[cid], n_test = "test", n_test + sizes[cid] elif n_train < 400: side[cid], n_train = "train", n_train + sizes[cid] Part Its one job Train fit the weights Validation choose: epochs, thresholds, prompts, learning rates Test one final measurement, by variety

slides.title: Count the labels for every department in every variety before training
slides.text: Measured in Lab 3.1 Count the labels for every department in every variety before training Department MSA Gulf Arabizi English billing 21 24 13 7 payments 18 3 7 9 connections 6 10 0 9 wastewater 19 18 1 3 Four cells of 32 have fewer than five training messages in this split. Each one is a promise the model cannot keep. Three honest answers: label more of exactly that kind, declare the cell unsupported, or send it to a person.

slides.title: A label is a decision someone made, and some were hard
slides.text: Label quality A label is a decision someone made, and some were hard CustomerMy bill is high and I think the meter is broken Labelledmeters CustomerThe pressure is weak and I have already paid the last bill Labelledsupply The first message is a billing complaint with a meters cause. Either label is defensible; an inconsistent one is not. The second carries a clause with another department's words. It is not the complaint. The model's ceiling is the labellers' agreement: measure it before training.

slides.title: Two labellers, 60 messages: 80% agree, and one cell holds most of the rest
slides.text: Label quality · complaint types in billing and payments Two labellers, 60 messages: 80% agree, and one cell holds most of the rest C \ D high bill duplicate charge payment failed high bill 27 2 0 duplicate charge 1 11 1 payment failed 1 7 10 Observed agreement: the diagonal, 48 of 60, 0.80. Chance agreement: labelling at their own rates without reading, 0.36. Half the messages are high bills. Kappa = (0.80 − 0.36) / (1 − 0.36) = 0.69. 7 of the 12 splits sit in one cell. That is a rule missing, not careless people.

slides.title: Fix the guideline, label the same sample again, then train
slides.text: Label quality · what to do with low agreement Fix the guideline, label the same sample again, then train The cell's messages "The amount left my card but the bill still shows unpaid." C read a failed payment; D read money taken twice. Guideline v2 adds one rule Money left, bill unpaid: payment failed. The same bill paid twice: duplicate charge. One example of each. Tempting move Why it fails Train anyway The model learns both readings Drop the split messages The hard cases leave the test set, not production A third labeller breaks ties The rule stays unwritten; the next labeller splits again Then measure again. The same 60, labelled blind by v2: 0.93 observed, kappa 0.89.

What is the honest status of that number? Too few runs: with twelve learning rates it would be reliable Fine, since the test messages were never used for training Optimistic: the test split chose the run, so it is no longer unseen Invalid: all six runs must be repeated on new data

slides.title: Fine-tuning an encoder
slides.text: Session 2 Fine-tuning an encoder Add a classification head to a pretrained encoder Fine-tune it with sensible defaults and watch validation Read a confusion matrix and name the errors 02

slides.title: A pretrained encoder, a mean over real tokens, and eight scores
slides.text: Fine-tuning an encoder A pretrained encoder, a mean over real tokens, and eight scores class Router(nn.Module): def __init__(self, encoder, n_labels): super().__init__() self.encoder = encoder self.drop = nn.Dropout(0.1) self.head = nn.Linear(encoder.cfg.d, n_labels) def forward(self, ids): mask = ids != 0 # padding out h = self.encoder(ids, mask) # a vector per token pooled = (h * mask[..., None]).sum(1) \ / mask.sum(1, keepdim=True) return self.head(self.drop(pooled)) The encoder arrives pretrained: it has read Sawaqi-style messages without labels. Pooling turns token vectors into one message vector. Padding is left out of the mean. The head is new: 128 × 8 weights and 8 biases. Full fine-tuning trains all 530,440 parameters.

slides.title: The training loop is the one you know, with two habits for small data
slides.text: Lab 3.2, step 2 The training loop is the one you know, with two habits for small data def train_epoch(model, opt, x, y): model.train() perm, total = torch.randperm(len(x)), 0.0 for s in range(0, len(x), 32): idx = perm[s:s + 32] loss = F.cross_entropy(model(x[idx]), y[idx]) opt.zero_grad() loss.backward() opt.step() total += loss.item() * len(idx) return total / len(x) Mask 15% of the input tokens Each epoch hides different tokens, as in pretraining. With 400 messages the model would otherwise learn single words by heart. Keep the best validation epoch Score the validation split after every epoch and keep those weights.

slides.title: The training loss keeps falling; the validation score stops
slides.text: Measured in Lab 3.2 · 40 epochs, about two minutes on a processor The training loss keeps falling; the validation score stops Epoch 5 10 15 20 25 30 35 40 Training loss 1.54 0.60 0.22 0.12 0.08 0.05 0.04 0.03 Validation macro F1 0.22 0.47 0.48 0.53 0.53 0.56 0.55 0.58 From epoch 20 the loss falls by a factor of four and validation moves within five points. The loop keeps the weights of the best validation epoch: here epoch 29. The test split has not been touched yet.

slides.title: Low-rank and quantised adapters
slides.text: Session 3 Low-rank and quantised adapters Explain the memory cost of full fine-tuning Write a low-rank adapter layer and count trainable parameters Compare an adapter run with full fine-tuning on the same split 03

slides.title: Training keeps every trainable weight four times
slides.text: Low-rank and quantised adapters Training keeps every trainable weight four times A weight that… Bytes during training trains (value, gradient, two Adam states) 16 is frozen, 32-bit 4 is frozen, 8-bit 1 is frozen, 4-bit 0.5 Model (gigabytes for the weights) Full Adapter, 32-bit Adapter, 4-bit Encoder, 110 million parameters 1.8 0.4 0.1 Decoder, 7 billion parameters 112 28.4 4.0 Adapters at 0.5% of the weights. Activations come on top and grow with the batch and the length of the text.

slides.title: Freeze the weight matrix; learn its change as two thin matrices
slides.text: The idea Freeze the weight matrix; learn its change as two thin matrices Frozen W 128 × 128 = 16,384 numbers ↓ A: 8 × 128 and B: 128 × 8 2,048 trainable numbers at rank 8 ↓ Output W x + (alpha / r) · B A x The bet: the change a task needs is low rank, so two thin matrices can hold it. B starts at zero : the adapted layer begins exactly as the pretrained one. Rank sets capacity; alpha / r scales the update. After training, add B A into W once: no extra latency when serving.

slides.title: The adapter layer is ten lines, and 1.7% of the model trains
slides.text: Lab 3.3, steps 1 and 2 The adapter layer is ten lines, and 1.7% of the model trains class LoRALinear(nn.Module): def __init__(self, base, r=8, alpha=16): super().__init__() self.base, self.scale = base, alpha / r for p in self.base.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False self.A = nn.Parameter( torch.randn(r, base.in_features) * 0.01) self.B = nn.Parameter( torch.zeros(base.out_features, r)) def forward(self, x): return self.base(x) \ + (x @ self.A.T @ self.B.T) * self.scale Course encoder with head Parameters Total 538,632 Adapters on query and value, 2 layers 8,192 The new head 1,032 Trainable 9,224 (1.7%)

slides.title: Frozen weights can be stored in fewer bits, at a small error
slides.text: Measured in Lab 3.3, step 3 Frozen weights can be stored in fewer bits, at a small error Run on the course encoder Megabytes for training In a 3 MB budget Full fine-tuning 8.49 no Adapter, 32-bit frozen weights 2.27 yes Adapter, 8-bit frozen weights 0.68 yes Quantising rounds each weight to one of 255 levels and keeps one scale per matrix. The frozen weights of the course encoder move by 2.5% on average. Only frozen weights can be held this way: a gradient step is smaller than one level. The adapters stay in 32 bits and learn on top of the rounded model.

slides.title: The adapter trains 1.7% of the weights and gives up 13 points
slides.text: Measured in Lab 3.3 · the evidence of LO4 The adapter trains 1.7% of the weights and gives up 13 points Run Trainable Macro F1 MSA Gulf Arabizi English Full fine-tuning (supplied) 530,440 0.63 0.68 0.66 0.28 0.59 Adapter, rank 8, 8-bit frozen weights 9,224 0.50 0.43 0.55 0.22 0.55 Same split, same 40 epochs, same token masking. The logs carry timestamps. At this size the saving is 8 megabytes, which nobody needs. The trade is real at 7 billion parameters, where full fine-tuning does not fit at all.

slides.title: Adapters are for a skill on a large model, not for facts and not for small models
slides.text: Using adapters well Adapters are for a skill on a large model, not for facts and not for small models Good fit A large model that does not fit your memory in full. Several tasks on one frozen model, one small adapter each. Poor fit A small model you can fine-tune in full. You pay quality and save nothing you need. Wrong tool Facts that change: prices, rules, dates. They belong in the rule book that Day 2 retrieves from.

slides.title: The tariff changes every quarter
slides.text: Checkpoint The tariff changes every quarter Latifa updates the tariff rule book four times a year. A colleague proposes a new low-rank adapter each quarter so that Ghayth "knows" the current prices. What do you answer? Yes, with a higher rank so that the adapter can hold the prices Yes, but with full fine-tuning, since adapters lose quality No: adapters over quantised weights would round the prices No: keep prices in the rule book and retrieve them; adapt for skills

The open question is Arabizi, and the only row that can answer it is yours.

slides.title: The decision is a function; the API is a thin layer over it
slides.text: Deploying The decision is a function; the API is a thin layer over it class Message(BaseModel): text: str = Field(max_length=2000) class Decision(BaseModel): department: Optional[str] confidence: float variety: str handoff: bool reason: Optional[str] account_number: Optional[str] district: Optional[str] @app.post("/route", response_model=Decision) def route(message: Message) -> Decision: return Decision(**decide(message.text)) FastAPI with Pydantic : the schema validates what comes in and what goes out, and documents the service. A message of 3,000 characters is refused with status 422 before the model runs. A demo page at the root lets a colleague try a message without a tool. Gradio or Streamlit do the same with more polish.

slides.title: The hand-off rule is part of the model, and it has a price
slides.text: Measured in Lab 3.4 · the baseline, as served The hand-off rule is part of the model, and it has a price Fewer than two words: no request. Best probability below 0.5, or 0.7 for Arabizi: low confidence. Second department at 60% of the first or more: two departments. This starting rule is right on every message it keeps, and keeps too few. Tuning it on validation data is the engineer's work; the trade is Hessa's decision. Variety Handed to a person Accuracy on the rest MSA 19% 1.00 Gulf 27% 1.00 English 41% 1.00 Arabizi 94% 1.00

slides.title: A smoke test proves the service is alive and sane at the edges
slides.text: Lab 3.4, step 2 A smoke test proves the service is alive and sane at the edges Case Must 20 real test messages, five per variety answer 200 with a department from the list An empty message be handed to a person Punctuation only A greeting with no request Three problems in one message 24 cases, a second to run, on every change. It says nothing about quality: that is the table by variety on the test split. The course's service passes: 24 of 24, with 18 of the 20 real messages sent to the right department.

slides.title: Measure latency through the service, not around the model
slides.text: Measured in Lab 3.4, step 3 Measure latency through the service, not around the model 4 ms the baseline alone, median (Lab 1.4) 25 ms through the service, median 31 ms through the service, 95th percentile; the budget is 300 ms The customer waits for validation, extraction, the model, the hand-off rule and the response. Report the median and the 95th percentile, on the hardware you will run on, and say which hardware.

slides.title: A model card says who the model fails, and what happens then
slides.text: The output of the course's labs A model card says who the model fails, and what happens then What it is for , and what it is not for. The served model and its data card. Results by language variety , as served, with the hand-off rate. The approaches compared : the table. Latency , and on what hardware. Limits : varieties below 0.7 macro F1. The hand-off rule , in plain words. Data and privacy : what is masked, and where. For this service "Arabizi messages are routed correctly far less often than the others. Almost all of them go to a person. Do not staff as if they were automated."

slides.title: One sentence about Arabizi
slides.text: Checkpoint One sentence about Arabizi The served router scores macro F1 0.85 overall and 0.42 for Arabizi, and hands 94% of Arabizi messages to a person. slides.title: Extraction and adaptation are scored on their evidence
slides.text: Two criteria, 20 points each Extraction and adaptation are scored on their evidence Extraction A masking test that passes: no account or phone number leaves. A schema whose validators reject wrong values. Precision and recall for each field, next to a pattern baseline. The log of validation failures, with what the service did. Adaptation A full fine-tuning run and a low-rank adapter run, same split. Trainable-parameter counts and the memory budget. Training logs with timestamps; the epoch chosen on validation. Test scores for both, by variety, and which one you would keep.

slides.title: Five criteria, 100 points
slides.text: How the repository is scored Five criteria, 100 points Three-way comparison 25% Extraction 20% Adaptation 20% Service and model card 20% Reproducibility 15% Pass: 70% overall, and at least 60% on this rubric. The repository is 60% of the result, the defence 20%, the supervised checks 20%.

slides.title: Eight minutes, then four minutes of questions
slides.text: The defence Eight minutes, then four minutes of questions 3 min · the table The task, the three rows by variety, and your recommendation. 3 min · a re-score The assessor gives a labelled batch you have not seen. Score your served model on it, live. 2 min · two errors Two messages from that batch your model got wrong: the cause of each, and the remedy. AI assistants were allowed in full. The defence is where you show that the decisions are yours.

slides.text: Before you publish Four things that cost marks, each checkable in a minute No baseline row, or no varieties One average hides the group the model fails. The test split chose something A threshold, a prompt, an epoch or a learning rate. Unmasked text left the machine An account or phone number in a prompt or a log. A number with no log Every figure in the README points at a committed file.
